title: Distributed Tracing
summary: The span/trace model, how context survives a hop across services, and how to read a waterfall to find where time actually went.

slides.markdown:
A **trace** represents one end-to-end request's journey through a system. It's made of **spans** — each span is one unit of work (an HTTP call, a DB query, a function) with a start time, duration, and metadata. Spans nest: a service handling a request creates a span, and if it calls a downstream service, that call becomes a **child span** — parent-child relationships that mirror the actual call graph.

A single user request through four services might produce a dozen spans, all sharing one trace ID, forming a tree that shows exactly how the work was structured.

For spans in different services to belong to the same trace, the **trace ID** (and the current span ID, as the new parent) must travel with the request itself — usually as HTTP headers (`traceparent` in the W3C Trace Context standard) carried across every network hop.

This is the mechanical crux of tracing: if a service makes an outbound call without forwarding that header, the chain breaks — the downstream service starts a *new*, disconnected trace instead of continuing the existing one, and the waterfall view loses that whole branch.

slides.sectionTitle: A trace waterfall across four services
slides.markdown:
A waterfall lays out every span as a horizontal bar — position shows when it started, width shows duration, indentation shows parent-child nesting.

![A trace waterfall across four services](assets/trace-waterfall.svg)

Reading one top to bottom answers "where did the time go": the widest bar is where the request spent its time, and gaps between a parent's span and its child reveal queuing delay pure code profiling would miss.

assets.alt: A trace waterfall across four services

slides.markdown:
Tracing every single request in a high-traffic system is often too expensive to store, so most systems sample.

| Strategy | Decision made | Trade-off |
|---|---|---|
| Head-based | At the start of the trace, before any spans are known | Cheap and simple, but might discard a trace that later turns out to be the interesting slow/error one |
| Tail-based | After the full trace completes, looking at its actual outcome | Can guarantee keeping every error/slow trace, but requires buffering the whole trace before deciding |

**How to decide:** tail-based sampling is strictly better for catching rare but important traces (errors, outliers) — the cost is the buffering infrastructure it requires.

Most tracing setups blend two sources: **automatic instrumentation** (an agent or library auto-generates spans for common operations — HTTP calls, DB queries — with zero code changes) and **manual spans** (a developer explicitly wraps a business-specific operation to make it visible, like "validate discount code").

Automatic instrumentation gets you 80% of the value for free; manual spans are what make a trace actually explain *your* domain logic instead of just generic framework calls.

Worked example: a checkout request takes 900ms and users are complaining. Opening its waterfall shows the gateway and auth spans are both fast (under 20ms each), but the Orders service's call into Inventory eats 650ms of the total — clearly the dominant cost. Without tracing, you'd have four services' worth of separate logs and metrics to cross-reference by hand; the waterfall shows it in one view.

Following that lead into Inventory's own spans reveals it's making a synchronous call to a third-party pricing API with no timeout — the actual root cause.

Tracing every single request in production sounds ideal — total visibility — but at real traffic volumes it can generate more span data than the tracing backend can ingest or afford to store, causing dropped spans, backend outages, or a bill nobody signed up for.

The fix is one of the sampling strategies above (tail-based is usually the sweet spot): keep everything interesting, sample the routine majority, rather than treating "trace everything" as free just because tracing infrastructure exists.
